exercises.instruction: Kéo để xếp các câu theo đúng 5 bước của khung (câu hỏi: Why do people enjoy spending time in natural places?).

exercises.title: Nói: trả lời câu WHY theo khung REASON × 3
exercises.instruction: 15 giây suy nghĩ, ghi âm nói 60–75 giây. Bắt đầu bằng câu báo trước nhiều lý do, nêu đủ ba tầng (tâm lý / thực tế / xã hội), mỗi lý do có một câu triển khai, và một câu kết luận.

items.prompt: Why do people take photographs of almost everything nowadays?
Why do people enjoy watching sport rather than playing it?

targetStructures: People do X for several reasons.
Psychologically speaking,… · From a practical standpoint,… · On a social level,…
For all these reasons, I think…
checklist: Câu mở báo trước sẽ có nhiều lý do
Có đủ ba tầng: tâm lý, thực tế, xã hội
Mỗi lý do có ít nhất một câu triển khai (ví dụ / hệ quả / so sánh)
Dùng ít nhất 2 cụm ★ (stems from, can be attributed to, a contributing factor is…)
Có câu kết luận, không dừng đột ngột; không dùng "because" quá 1 lần
commonErrors: Ba lý do đều cùng một tầng
Dùng "because" năm lần trong một câu trả lời
Nêu lý do rồi dừng, không triển khai
Trả lời bằng trải nghiệm cá nhân ("Because I like it")
rubric.sampleAnswer: People photograph almost everything now for several interconnected reasons. Psychologically speaking, taking a picture gives a sense of holding onto a moment that would otherwise slip away — it's a very human response to the feeling that time passes too quickly. From a practical standpoint, the barrier has essentially disappeared: everyone carries a high-quality camera, storage is effectively unlimited, and it costs nothing, so there's no reason not to. And on a social level, photos have become a form of communication in themselves — a way of showing where you are and who you're with, rather than describing it. For all these reasons, I think the habit is less about photography in the traditional sense and more about documenting and sharing a life.

exercises.title: Khung NUANCED OPINION
exercises.instruction: Chọn đáp án đúng.

items.prompt: Cách trả lời nào MẤT điểm nặng nhất ở câu Opinion?

options.text: Nêu hai mặt rồi chốt bên có điều kiện

items.explanation: Không có lập luận, giám khảo phải hỏi lại.

items.prompt: Khung NUANCED OPINION là:

items.prompt: Câu kết Opinion nên là:

options.text: Một câu tóm tắt lại cả hai mặt
Một câu chọn bên NHƯNG có điều kiện ("…, provided that…" / "…only when…")

items.prompt: Hedging chồng chất ("Maybe it can perhaps possibly be quite good") bị lỗi gì?

options.text: tôi chưa đến mức nói rằng…

On one hand, the cognitive benefits are well-established — reading notation and sustaining focus transfer to academic performance.
answer: To a certain extent, yes — but I'd stop short of saying it should be compulsory for everyone.
On one hand, the cognitive benefits are well-established — reading notation and sustaining focus transfer to academic performance.
On the other hand, forcing every child to learn an instrument could easily backfire and create resentment rather than appreciation.
On balance, music education is valuable, but its benefits only really materialise when children engage with it willingly.
items.explanation: SẮC THÁI → MỘT MẶT → MẶT KIA → CÂN BẰNG (kết luận có điều kiện).

exercises.title: Chuyển Yes/No thành câu có sắc thái
exercises.instruction: Gõ lại câu đã sửa / nâng cấp theo mẫu (gõ từng chữ, có gợi ý). Viết lại mỗi câu trả lời nghèo nàn thành một câu mở có sắc thái, dùng cụm hedging.

items.prompt: Yes, technology is good.
items.explanation: Trả lời câu hỏi nhưng không tuyệt đối.
sampleAnswers: Generally speaking, technology has been beneficial, but it depends on how it is used.

items.prompt: No, exams are not useful.
items.explanation: Nêu sắc thái thay vì phủ định thẳng.
sampleAnswers: To a certain extent exams are useful, but I would stop short of saying they measure everything that matters.

items.prompt: Yes, everyone should recycle.
items.explanation: Chọn bên nhưng thừa nhận giới hạn.
sampleAnswers: On balance recycling is worthwhile, though its impact is often overstated.

items.prompt: Although it is expensive, but it is worth it.
items.explanation: Không dùng although và but cùng lúc.
sampleAnswers: Although it is expensive, it is worth it.

exercises.title: Nói: trả lời câu Opinion có sắc thái
exercises.instruction: 15 giây suy nghĩ, ghi âm nói 60–80 giây. Câu mở phải có sắc thái (KHÔNG Yes/No đơn lẻ), nêu một mặt ủng hộ có ví dụ và một mặt giới hạn, kết bằng câu chọn bên có điều kiện.

items.prompt: Do you think people today are happier than people were fifty years ago?
Do you think it is important for adults to keep learning new skills?

targetStructures: To a certain extent, yes — but I would stop short of saying…
On one hand,… (+ ví dụ) → On the other hand,… (+ ví dụ)
On balance, I believe…, provided that… / …only when…
checklist: Câu mở có sắc thái, không phải Yes/No
Có ít nhất một lập luận ủng hộ có ví dụ
Có ít nhất một lập luận giới hạn
Dùng ít nhất 2 cụm hedging
Kết luận có chọn bên VÀ có điều kiện kèm theo; không dùng "I think" quá 2 lần
commonErrors: Trả lời "Yes, I think so." rồi im
Nói cực đoan một chiều
Dùng "I think" mở đầu năm câu liên tiếp
Nêu hai mặt nhưng không chọn bên nào ở cuối
rubric.sampleAnswer: To a certain extent, yes, but I'd stop short of saying it's a straightforward improvement. On one hand, people today have access to things that materially improve quality of life — better healthcare, more personal freedom, and far more choice in how they live. Someone with a chronic illness fifty years ago simply had fewer options. On the other hand, rates of anxiety and loneliness appear to have risen, partly because the same freedom that expands choice also removes the ready-made communities people used to belong to. On balance, I'd say people are better off in objective terms, but whether they feel happier depends heavily on whether they've managed to rebuild the sense of belonging that older, less mobile societies provided by default.

exercises.title: Khung BENEFIT–DRAWBACK–BALANCE
exercises.instruction: Chọn đáp án đúng.

items.prompt: Thế nào là một BẤT LỢI THẬT?

Một danh sách 5 bất lợi liệt kê nhanh

items.prompt: Câu hỏi "What are the drawbacks of standardised testing?" thuộc dạng:

exercises.title: Xếp câu trả lời theo khung BENEFIT–DRAWBACK–BALANCE
exercises.instruction: Kéo để xếp các câu theo đúng 4 bước (câu hỏi: advantages and disadvantages of working from home).

On balance, the benefits outweigh the drawbacks, provided that companies deliberately design in the contact that used to happen naturally.
The main benefit is autonomy — people organise their day around when they work best, and in a big city the recovered commuting time can be two hours a day.
answer: Remote working is very much a double-edged sword.

exercises.title: Nói: trả lời câu Advantages / Disadvantages
exercises.instruction: 15 giây suy nghĩ, ghi âm nói 70–90 giây. Nêu hai lợi ích (ít nhất một có ví dụ), một bất lợi THẬT có người chịu thiệt, dùng while hoặc whereas, và kết bằng điều kiện đánh đổi.

items.prompt: What are the advantages and disadvantages of children using tablets at school?
What are the advantages and disadvantages of tourism for a small town?

targetStructures: [X] brings both clear benefits and some real drawbacks / is a double-edged sword.
The main benefit is… · A significant drawback is…
While A…, B… · On balance, …, provided that…
checklist: Câu mở báo trước hai mặt
Có hai lợi ích, ít nhất một có ví dụ
Bất lợi nêu rõ ai chịu thiệt (có cơ chế cụ thể)
Dùng while hoặc whereas ít nhất một lần
Kết luận có điều kiện, không đếm số lượng
commonErrors: Liệt kê 5 lợi ích và 5 bất lợi kiểu danh sách
Bất lợi giả: "The disadvantage is that it is not perfect."
Kết luận kiểu đếm: "three advantages and two disadvantages, so it is good"
Nhầm sang dạng Opinion
rubric.sampleAnswer: Using tablets in class is very much a double-edged sword. The main benefit is access — a single device replaces a whole shelf of textbooks, and interactive material can adapt to a child's level in a way a printed page can't. There's also an equity argument: schools that lend devices can put resources in the hands of children whose families couldn't afford them. That said, it comes at a cost. A significant drawback is that constant screen access makes sustained attention harder, and the children hit hardest are those who already struggle to focus — for them the tablet becomes a source of distraction rather than learning. On balance, I'd say tablets are worth using, provided that schools are deliberate about when screens are on and when they're off, rather than treating the device as a default.

exercises.title: Khung COMPARE FRAMEWORK

items.prompt: "So sánh theo hàng" nghĩa là:

options.text: Mô tả xong hết A rồi mới sang B
So sánh A và B theo TỪNG KHÍA CẠNH một (tốc độ, chi phí…), mỗi khía cạnh nói cả A lẫn B

items.explanation: Nói theo cột (hết A rồi B) làm người nghe phải tự ghép → mất Coherence.

items.prompt: Dấu hiệu Band 7+ trong câu so sánh là:

options.text: Nêu được một ĐIỂM CHUNG giữa hai đối tượng đối lập
Mô tả thật nhiều chi tiết A

Chọn ra MỘT khác biệt quan trọng nhất ("the most significant shift is in…")

exercises.instruction: Viết lại cả câu cho đúng.

items.prompt: This is not as good like the old system.

exercises.title: Nói: trả lời câu Compare / Contrast
exercises.instruction: 15 giây suy nghĩ, ghi âm nói 70–90 giây. So sánh theo KHÍA CẠNH (ít nhất 2), nêu một điểm chung, và kết bằng nhận định về khác biệt quan trọng nhất. Không dùng "better".

items.prompt: How is the way people communicate with friends today different from twenty years ago?
How is city life different from life in the countryside?

targetStructures: …differ in several significant ways / …has undergone a dramatic transformation
In terms of…, A… whereas B… · By comparison,…
That said, they share some common ground… → Ultimately, the most significant shift is in…
checklist: So sánh theo khía cạnh, không mô tả lần lượt hai đối tượng
Nêu rõ ít nhất hai khía cạnh (tốc độ / chi phí / con người / quyền lực)
Dùng ít nhất 2 cụm ★ (in terms of, by comparison, nowhere near as…)
Có nêu một điểm chung
Câu kết chọn một khác biệt quan trọng nhất; không dùng "better"
commonErrors: Mô tả xong hết A rồi mới sang B
Chỉ dùng "more" và "better": "more better and more convenient"
So sánh mà không nói rõ so sánh về mặt gì
Quên hoàn toàn điểm chung
rubric.sampleAnswer: The way friends communicate has changed considerably over the past twenty years, mainly because of smartphones. In terms of frequency, contact used to be occasional — a phone call or a meet-up — whereas now it's almost continuous, a low-level stream of messages throughout the day. In terms of depth, though, the picture is more mixed: earlier conversations were fewer but longer and more focused, whereas a lot of messaging today is fragmented and easy to half-ignore. That said, the two still share common ground — when something serious happens, people still reach for a call, because they instinctively know text isn't enough. Ultimately, the most significant shift is that friendship no longer requires deliberate effort to maintain contact, which sounds convenient but arguably makes each individual exchange feel less valuable.

exercises.title: Khung Problem / Solution & vai trò chính phủ
exercises.instruction: Chọn đáp án đúng.

items.prompt: Giải pháp "People should be more aware" bị lỗi gì?

options.text: Không có CHỦ THỂ — ai làm cho họ nhận thức, bằng cách nào?

items.explanation: Mỗi giải pháp phải trả lời AI LÀM và LÀM GÌ.

items.prompt: Kẹt xe ở đô thị — đâu là NGUYÊN NHÂN GỐC (không phải triệu chứng)?

options.text: Có quá nhiều xe máy trên đường
Nhà ở gần nơi làm việc quá đắt nên người ta phải đi làm xa
Mọi người ra khỏi nhà cùng một giờ

items.explanation: Nguyên nhân cấu trúc, không phải triệu chứng bề mặt.

items.prompt: Khung 5B (câu hỏi về chính phủ) gồm:

exercises.instruction: 15 giây suy nghĩ, ghi âm nói 75–90 giây. Nêu nguyên nhân GỐC (không phải triệu chứng), một giải pháp CÓ CHỦ THỂ rõ ràng, một giới hạn của giải pháp, và một câu về trách nhiệm nhiều bên.

rubric.sampleAnswer: The root cause of workplace stress, I think, isn't individual time management but the way work is structured. In many organisations, staff are given more responsibility than the hours actually allow, and the culture treats long hours as a sign of commitment. A more effective approach might be for employers to redesign workloads around realistic capacity and to protect time off explicitly — but that has to come from senior management, not from individual employees, because a single person taking evenings off in a culture that rewards overwork simply falls behind. Of course, that alone wouldn't solve everything, because some stress comes from economic insecurity that no employer can fix. Ultimately it requires a combination of company policy, sensible regulation on working hours, and a broader cultural shift away from equating exhaustion with dedication.

rubric.sampleAnswer: The way people spend their free time has shifted noticeably over the past few decades. It used to be organised around shared physical activities — sport, cinemas, visiting relatives. Today, by comparison, a large share of leisure time is spent alone with a screen, streaming or scrolling. This shift is largely driven by two things: the affordability of devices and the way entertainment platforms are engineered to hold attention. If this continues, it seems likely that leisure will become even more personalised and on-demand, with fewer fixed schedules. That said, it is difficult to predict with any certainty, because there are early signs of a backlash — a growing interest in offline hobbies and 'digital detox'. A more cautious view might be that we settle into a mix, using screens for convenience but deliberately protecting some time for the shared, physical activities people seem to miss.

rubric.sampleAnswer: That's a 'why' question, so I'll give a few reasons at different levels. Psychologically, some students carry a heavier fear of failure — often tied to how their family talks about grades — and that anxiety actually interferes with performance rather than driving it. From a practical standpoint, out-of-school support is unevenly distributed: a child with quiet study space and access to private tuition has a structural advantage over one who doesn't, regardless of ability. And on a social level, classrooms tend to develop expectations — a student labelled early as 'weak' often internalises that and disengages. For all these reasons, I'd argue that gaps within a single class are less about raw talent and more about the conditions surrounding the child, which is why a genuinely student-centred approach tries to identify and remove those specific obstacles.

rubric.sampleAnswer: To a certain extent, yes, but I don't think it's as simple as over-reliance. In some respects the smartphone has clearly reduced effort: navigation apps mean we don't memorise routes, autocorrect compensates for weak spelling, and translation apps do a lot of work that used to require real study. There is a reasonable argument that this steady reduction in friction lowers our tolerance for difficulty. However, I would push back on calling that dependence, because the same device also frees up attention that routine tasks used to consume — whether people spend that freed-up time well is a question of discipline, not of the phone. On balance, I'd say the smartphone amplifies existing tendencies rather than creating new ones: a motivated person uses it to do more, and a distracted person uses it to avoid things. The tool is fairly neutral — the user isn't.

a disproportionate share of emissions comes from a small number of industrial actors
individual action is necessary but not sufficient

rubric.sampleAnswer: There are a few reasons, and they operate at different levels. Psychologically, the threat feels abstract and distant — biodiversity loss and rising emissions don't produce an immediate, visible consequence for most people, so the brain deprioritises them. From a practical standpoint, acting sustainably often costs more or takes more effort, and for households already under financial pressure that trade-off isn't realistic. And on a systemic level, there's a fair amount of greenwashing, which leaves people cynical about whether anything they do matters. It's also worth noting that responsibility is often framed as purely individual, when a disproportionate share of emissions actually comes from a small number of large industrial actors. So I'd say the indifference is partly rational: people sense that individual action is necessary but not sufficient, and without visible stringent regulation, the incentive to bother is weak.

rubric.sampleAnswer: There are a few structural reasons. Urbanisation means most people now live where the work is rather than where their family is, so the neighbourhood is a temporary base, not a community. Digital connectivity partly fills the gap, but online contact tends to be with people who are already friends, not with the person next door. And mobile lifestyles — the fact that people move every few years — means nobody has the incentive to invest in local relationships that they'll leave behind anyway. The result is measurable: higher loneliness and lower social trust. I'd also add that the capacity to engage is heavily shaped by economic circumstances — someone working long hours or two jobs simply doesn't have the evenings free that neighbourly contact tends to require, so this isn't really a question of people caring less.

rubric.sampleAnswer: It's tempting to say people just don't manage their time well, but the reasons are more structural. Time pressure is the main one: in economies where long hours are normalised and commuting eats up two hours a day, the space for recovery simply isn't there. There's also a cost dimension — proper time off, counselling, or even a quieter place to live all cost money, so the people most exposed to work-related stress are often least able to buy their way out of it. And the environment reinforces it: if a workplace culture treats being constantly available as a sign of commitment, then switching off carries a real career risk. If employers rewarded output rather than hours, a lot of this would ease. So I'd argue the solution is less about individual resilience and more about redesigning the environment in which people make these decisions.

rubric.sampleAnswer: Too many tourists tend to cause problems that fall on residents rather than on the town as a whole. Economically, the benefits are real but unevenly distributed — a significant proportion is captured by property owners and large operators, while ordinary residents face the downsides. exercises.instruction: 15 giây suy nghĩ, ghi âm nói 80–95 giây. Nêu CƠ CHẾ (engagement-driven design), có cả mặt trao quyền và mặt gây hại, dùng thuật ngữ chính xác (không nói "fake news" cho mọi thứ), và có ít nhất một mệnh đề nhượng bộ nâng cao.

Nói "fake news" cho mọi vấn đề thông tin
Mô tả hành vi mà không nói vì sao nền tảng khuyến khích nó

rubric.sampleAnswer: It spreads quickly because the structure of the platforms rewards it. These systems are designed to maximise engagement rather than well-being, so an algorithmically curated feed favours whatever provokes a strong reaction — and false or exaggerated claims tend to be more surprising, and therefore more shareable, than careful corrections. There's also a timing asymmetry: a dramatic claim reaches a large audience within hours, whereas a fact-check arrives days later to a fraction of the same people. Add algorithmic bias and echo chambers, and users mostly encounter information that already fits their existing beliefs, which lowers their guard. Whilst it's true that the same openness has given genuine visibility to marginalised voices and enabled real citizen journalism, the same mechanism that empowers those voices also accelerates misinformation — the design doesn't distinguish between the two.

rubric.sampleAnswer: It largely comes down to whether an art form can find a place in the modern economy. Traditional forms that can be adapted for performance, tourism or teaching tend to survive, because they generate revenue that funds their continuation. Forms that depended on a specific social ritual — a particular festival, a craft tied to a way of life that no longer exists — lose their function and fade, because the market simply doesn't price the social value they carried. Economically, younger people migrate to cities for work and the apprenticeship chains that transmitted these skills break. It's worth adding that this isn't uniform: in societies with strong state heritage protection or a deliberate cultural policy, forms survive that would disappear elsewhere. So the real question is not so much whether a tradition is 'valuable' as whether anyone has created the conditions — funding, teaching, visibility — in which it can still be practised.

items.prompt: 1. Why do so many young people want to go to university?
2. Do you think a university degree is still necessary to get a good job?

4. How is the job market today different from your parents' generation?
5. How do you think work will change in the next twenty years?

checklist: Fluency & Coherence: mỗi câu 60–90 giây, không dừng quá 3 giây

Grammatical Range: câu phức, bị động, mệnh đề quan hệ; lỗi không cản trở hiểu

rubric.sampleAnswer:
BÀI MẪU BAND 7.5–8 — BỘ ĐỀ 1: EDUCATION & WORK (mỗi câu 60–90 giây, đúng khung của dạng)

1. Why do so many young people want to go to university? (REASON × 3)
"There are several reasons, at different levels. Psychologically, university has become part of the expected life path — for many families, not going feels like falling behind. From a practical standpoint, a lot of well-paid careers still use a degree as a basic filter, so it functions as a gateway regardless of what you actually learn. And on a social level, it's also about the experience — moving away from home, building a network, and a few years of relative freedom before full-time work. So the degree itself is only part of the appeal."

2. Do you think a university degree is still necessary to get a good job? (NUANCED OPINION)
"To a certain extent, but less than it used to be. On one hand, in fields like medicine, law or engineering it's still essential, and many employers use it to filter applications. On the other hand, in areas like tech, design or digital marketing, a strong portfolio and demonstrated skills increasingly matter more than the qualification. On balance, a degree still helps, but it's no longer the guarantee it once was — it's necessary in some fields and merely useful in others."

3. What are the advantages and disadvantages of studying while working? (BENEFIT–DRAWBACK–BALANCE)
"It's very much a double-edged sword. The main benefit is that you apply what you learn immediately, so the knowledge sticks, and you graduate with real experience and no debt. That said, a significant drawback is the strain: something usually suffers — grades, work performance, or health — and the people hit hardest are those without a supportive employer who can offer flexible hours. On balance, it works well provided the workload is genuinely manageable and the employer is on board."

4. How is the job market today different from your parents' generation? (COMPARE)
"It's changed considerably. In terms of security, my parents' generation could expect one employer, a clear promotion ladder and a pension, whereas now people change jobs every few years and job security is much weaker. In terms of skills, a qualification used to last a career, whereas today continuous retraining is more or less mandatory. That said, the two share common ground — both generations work hard and value being good at what they do. Ultimately, the biggest shift is that responsibility for a career has moved from the employer to the individual."

5. How do you think work will change in the next twenty years? (TREND–PREDICTION–CAVEAT)
"Looking at current trends, the clearest change will probably be driven by automation. Routine tasks are likely to be largely automated, which will shift human work towards judgement, creativity and managing the technology itself. We may also see the standard week become shorter or more flexible, given how much remote work has already normalised. That said, it's difficult to predict with any certainty, because these shifts depend heavily on regulation and on how businesses share the gains. A more cautious view is that change will be slower and more uneven than the headlines suggest."

exercises.title: THI THỬ — Bộ đề 2: Environment & Community
exercises.instruction: Giám khảo hỏi liên tiếp, không dừng giữa chừng. Ghi âm trả lời cả 5 câu, mỗi câu 60–90 giây. Nhận đúng dạng và dùng đúng khung.

items.prompt: 1. Why are some people not interested in environmental issues?
2. Do you think individuals can make a real difference to the environment?
3. What can local governments do to reduce waste in cities?
4. How have attitudes towards the environment changed in your country?
5. Will cities be greener or more polluted in fifty years?

targetStructures: REASON × 3 (câu 1) · NUANCED OPINION (câu 2) · CAUSE–EFFECT–SOLUTION (câu 3)
COMPARE / THEN–NOW–NEXT (câu 4) · TREND–PREDICTION–CAVEAT (câu 5)
necessary but not sufficient · a more effective approach might be · driven by / a more cautious view might be
checklist: Mỗi câu 60–90 giây, không dừng quá 3 giây
≥3 cụm ★ chuyên đề Environment / Society mỗi câu, dùng đúng thuật ngữ
Câu 2: có cả trục cá nhân và hệ thống · Câu 3: giải pháp có chủ thể + giới hạn
Câu 5: dự đoán có lực đẩy + caveat có lý do, không dùng "will" trần
Nhận đúng dạng cả 5 câu; có câu kết mỗi câu
commonErrors: Khẩu hiệu rỗng ("protect the environment for future generations")
Giải pháp không có chủ thể
Dự đoán trống, không có lực đẩy
Trả lời câu đầu quá dài rồi hụt hơi
rubric.sampleAnswer:
BÀI MẪU BAND 8 — BỘ ĐỀ 2: ENVIRONMENT & COMMUNITY

1. Why are some people not interested in environmental issues? (REASON × 3)
"There are a few structural reasons. Psychologically, the threat feels abstract and distant — biodiversity loss and rising emissions don't produce an immediate, visible consequence, so the brain deprioritises them. From a practical standpoint, acting sustainably often costs more or takes more effort, and for households already under financial pressure that trade-off isn't realistic. And on a social level, a lot of greenwashing has left people cynical about whether anything they do matters. So the indifference is partly rational: people sense that individual action is necessary but not sufficient."

2. Do you think individuals can make a real difference to the environment? (NUANCED OPINION)
"Individuals can make a meaningful difference, but it's worth being honest about the limits of individual action in isolation. On one hand, collective behaviour drives markets — when enough consumers refuse single-use plastics, producers adapt. On the other hand, a disproportionate share of global emissions comes from a small number of industrial actors, and framing the problem as purely personal can function as a deflection. On balance, individual action works best as part of a broader ecosystem of change that includes stringent regulation and corporate accountability."

3. What can local governments do to reduce waste in cities? (CAUSE–EFFECT–SOLUTION)
"The root cause is that waste is currently cheaper to produce than to avoid, so the incentives are wrong. A more effective approach might be for city governments to make producers responsible for packaging through deposit-return schemes and to invest properly in separated collection and composting — households can only recycle what the system actually processes. Of course, that alone wouldn't solve everything, because many packaging decisions are made at national or corporate level. Ultimately it needs city policy, national regulation and consumer habits working together."

4. How have attitudes towards the environment changed in your country? (THEN–NOW–NEXT / COMPARE)
"They've shifted noticeably over the past couple of decades. It used to be a fringe concern discussed mainly by activists, whereas today it's fairly mainstream — recycling is normal, and younger people in particular factor it into everyday choices. This shift is largely driven by more visible extreme weather and by international pressure. That said, awareness hasn't fully translated into behaviour or policy, partly because economic growth is still the overriding priority. A more cautious view is that the change is real but shallow."

5. Will cities be greener or more polluted in fifty years? (TREND–PREDICTION–CAVEAT)
"I think the most likely outcome is greener, but very unevenly. Wealthier cities are already retrofitting for heat and flooding, so we're likely to see a rapid expansion of green space, vertical planting and cleaner transport, driven mainly by climate pressure. Poorer, fast-growing cities may struggle to keep pace and could get worse before they improve. That said, it's difficult to predict with any certainty. On balance, I'd expect the average city to be cleaner than today, but the gap between rich and poor cities to widen."

exercises.title: THI THỬ — Bộ đề 3: Technology & Society
exercises.instruction: Giám khảo hỏi liên tiếp, không dừng giữa chừng. Ghi âm trả lời cả 5 câu, mỗi câu 60–90 giây. Nhận đúng dạng và dùng đúng khung.

items.prompt: 1. Why do people spend so much time on social media?
2. Do you think technology has brought people closer together?
3. What are the benefits and drawbacks of working with artificial intelligence?
4. How is the way people make friends today different from in the past?
5. How might communication change in the next generation?

targetStructures: REASON × 3 (câu 1) · NUANCED OPINION (câu 2) · BENEFIT–DRAWBACK–BALANCE (câu 3)
COMPARE FRAMEWORK (câu 4) · TREND–PREDICTION–CAVEAT (câu 5)

checklist: Mỗi câu 60–90 giây, không dừng quá 3 giây
≥3 cụm ★ chuyên đề Technology / Media mỗi câu, thuật ngữ chính xác

Nhận đúng dạng cả 5 câu; có câu kết mỗi câu

Dùng "technology" như một khối duy nhất
Nói "fake news" cho mọi vấn đề thông tin
Bỏ câu kết ở những câu cuối vì mệt
rubric.sampleAnswer:
BÀI MẪU BAND 8 — BỘ ĐỀ 3: TECHNOLOGY & SOCIETY

1. Why do people spend so much time on social media? (REASON × 3)
"For several interconnected reasons. Psychologically, these platforms are designed to maximise engagement, not well-being — an algorithmically curated feed delivers small, unpredictable rewards that are genuinely hard to put down. From a practical standpoint, a lot of social and even professional life now happens there, so stepping away has a real cost. And on a social level, there's a fear of missing out — if your friends are all coordinating and sharing on a platform, opting out means opting out of the group. So it's less pure choice than it looks."

2. Do you think technology has brought people closer together? (NUANCED OPINION)
"To a certain extent, but it's more nuanced than a simple yes. On one hand, it has removed almost all the barriers to staying in touch — people maintain friendships across continents with minimal effort, and marginalised groups have found communities they could never have found offline. On the other hand, the same tools can make relationships shallower: a stream of low-effort messages isn't the same as sustained attention, and public broadcasting has replaced a lot of private conversation. On balance, technology has increased the quantity of connection while putting the quality under strain."

3. What are the benefits and drawbacks of working with artificial intelligence? (BENEFIT–DRAWBACK–BALANCE)
"AI is very much a double-edged sword. The main benefit is that it frees up cognitive bandwidth — it handles routine drafting, summarising and analysis, letting people focus on judgement and creative work, and there's a productivity gain that can lower costs. That said, a significant drawback is deskilling: if junior staff never do the basic work themselves, they may not develop the judgement to check the AI's output, and they're the group hit hardest. On balance, the benefits outweigh the drawbacks provided organisations are deliberate about keeping humans genuinely in the loop."

4. How is the way people make friends today different from in the past? (COMPARE)
"It's changed in a couple of significant ways. In terms of where friendships start, they used to form almost entirely through proximity — school, work, the neighbourhood — whereas now a large share begin online, around shared interests rather than shared location. In terms of maintenance, friendship used to require deliberate effort to stay in contact, whereas now a low level of contact happens passively through feeds and group chats. That said, they share common ground — people still value a small number of close, trusted friends above a large network. Ultimately, the biggest shift is that geography matters far less than it did."

5. How might communication change in the next generation? (TREND–PREDICTION–CAVEAT)
"Looking at current trends, communication is likely to become even more instant, visual and asynchronous — shorter messages, more voice notes and video, less real-time conversation. We may also see AI increasingly mediating messages — drafting, translating, summarising — which could smooth communication across languages but also make it harder to know what's genuinely a person's own voice. That said, it's difficult to predict with any certainty, and there are early signs of a counter-trend, with some people deliberately choosing slower, more personal forms of contact. On balance, I'd expect faster and more convenient communication, with a small but real backlash in favour of depth."
